title: Demonstrate understanding of everyday aural texts in X

lessons.title: What aural texts are and how to listen
lessons.html:
What aural texts are

Aural means to do with hearing. An aural text is anything you listen to: a person speaking, a radio programme, an announcement, a voice note, a phone call, a song or a story told aloud. This unit is about listening carefully and showing that you understand what you heard, in your chosen language (X).

Aural texts at work and at home

  • Instructions from your supervisor at the start of the day.
  • A safety talk (toolbox talk).
  • Announcements over a loudspeaker or radio.
  • Phone calls and voice notes from clients or the office.
  • Weather forecasts on the radio.
  • News and community notices on local radio.
  • Stories, songs and speeches.

Why listening matters

If you do not listen well, mistakes happen. A team plants the wrong plants in the wrong bed. A worker misses the warning that a storm is coming. A client's message is lost. In horticulture, a missed instruction about spraying or watering can kill plants or harm people.

How to listen well

  1. Get ready. Stop other work. Move away from noise, like a running lawnmower.
  2. Listen for the purpose. Is it giving information, an instruction, a warning, or entertainment?
  3. Listen for key words: names, places, numbers, times, and words like must, never, first, then.
  4. Make notes of important details if you can.
  5. Ask if something is not clear. With a recording or radio, play it again if possible.

Example

The supervisor says: Today team A is on the hotel job. First cut the front lawn, then trim the hedges along the parking. Do not water today, the client says the borehole is low.

Key details: team A, hotel, lawn first, then hedges at the parking, no watering because the borehole is low.

lessons.title: Showing that you understood
lessons.html:
Showing that you understood

Main idea and details

After listening, you should be able to say:

  • The main idea: what the text was mostly about.
  • The important details: who, what, where, when, how many.
  • What you must do, if anything.

Ways to show understanding

  • Repeat the message in your own words.
  • Answer questions about it.
  • Pass the message on correctly to someone else.
  • Write down the important details.
  • Do the task correctly.

Passing on a message

Messages often change as they pass from person to person. To pass a message correctly:

  1. Write it down when you hear it.
  2. Include who it is from, who it is for, the date and time.
  3. Give the exact facts: numbers, names, places.
  4. Pass it on as soon as you can.

Tone and feeling

The way a person speaks tells you how they feel. A fast, loud voice may mean they are worried or angry. A slow, soft voice may mean they are tired or sad. A warning is usually said firmly. Listening to tone helps you respond in the right way.

Fact and opinion in what you hear

Radio adverts and speakers often mix facts and opinions. Rain is expected in Gauteng tomorrow is a fact from the forecast. This is the best weed killer ever is an opinion. Think about what you hear before you believe it.

Responding

  • Say thank you or okay to show you received the message.
  • Ask a question to check details.
  • Give your view politely if asked.

Key points

  • Aural texts are anything you listen to: instructions, radio, calls, stories.
  • Get ready, cut out noise and listen for key words.
  • Be able to give the main idea, the details and what you must do.
  • Write down messages and pass them on with exact facts.
  • Listen to tone, and tell facts apart from opinions.
